paragraphs: A robust Markov decision process seeks a policy that remains reliable when the environment changes within the uncertainty represented by the problem. This paper studies policy gradient methods for the s-rectangular version of that framework. Earlier methods required many iterations to reach a globally optimal solution to a chosen accuracy, while their guarantees relied on exact gradients and small state spaces.

The authors introduce an accelerated algorithm using entropy regularization. In the deterministic setting, its iteration complexity is O(ε⁻³ ln ε⁻¹), improving on the stated previous requirement of at least O(ε⁻⁴). Here, ε specifies the desired accuracy, so the result describes how the required optimization work grows as the accuracy requirement becomes stricter.

The paper also extends the method to large state spaces and stochastic gradients, obtaining sample complexity O(ε⁻⁷ ln ε⁻¹). This is a separate guarantee about samples rather than iterations. Together, the results broaden the settings covered by robust policy gradient theory and provide scalable methods for entropy-regularized robust decision problems.
icml-2024-accelerated-policy-gradient-fo.tldr: An entropy-regularized policy gradient method improves theoretical iteration complexity for robust MDPs and extends to stochastic gradients and large state spaces.

paragraphs: Momentum can accelerate optimization, but its benefits for reinforcement learning policy gradients have lacked a clear theoretical account. This paper adapts Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method to policy optimization, calling the resulting algorithm Accelerated Policy Gradient, or APG. Its central question is how quickly this approach can reach an optimal policy.

With access to the true gradient and a softmax policy parameterization, the authors prove two convergence rates. Nearly constant step sizes yield a rate of approximately 1/t², up to logarithmic factors, while time-varying step sizes yield exponential decay in the error. These guarantees depend on the stated gradient and parameterization setting.

The analysis explains why momentum can help: regardless of initialization, APG enters a locally nearly concave region after finitely many iterations. Within that region, the optimization landscape supports acceleration. Numerical validation and Atari 2600 experiments support the reported convergence behavior and improvements over standard policy gradient. The contribution combines rate guarantees with an explanation of the regime that makes them possible.
icml-2024-accelerated-policy-gradient-on.tldr: APG adapts Nesterov momentum to policy learning and proves accelerated convergence under true gradients and softmax policy parameterization.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of a complex-valued signal from repeated sets of measurements corrupted by speckle noise. Speckle is multiplicative: the noise interacts with the signal rather than simply adding a separate disturbance. Each measurement set is called a look, and the work examines both the accuracy of likelihood-based recovery and practical algorithms for performing it.

The theoretical contribution is an upper bound on the mean squared error of maximum likelihood estimation under the deep image prior hypothesis. The bound tracks how reconstruction error depends on the prior’s parameter count, the number of looks, the signal dimension, and the measurements available in each look. This makes the relationship between model size, measurement resources, and recovery accuracy explicit.

For computation, the authors introduce Bagged-DIP and combine it with projected gradient descent. They also use the Newton–Schulz algorithm to calculate matrix inverses inside the optimization iterations, reducing computational complexity. The abstract reports state-of-the-art performance, pairing that algorithmic result with a theoretical account of reconstruction error.
icml-2024-bagged-deep-image-prior-for-re.tldr: Bagged-DIP combines likelihood-based recovery, deep image priors, and cheaper matrix inversion to reconstruct signals affected by speckle noise.

paragraphs: CogDPM connects diffusion models with predictive coding, a cognitive theory of how predictions help organize visual processing over space and time. Earlier prediction networks inspired by this theory used hierarchical learning and corrections based on prediction residuals. According to the paper, they did not demonstrate improved forecasting on real-world tasks and omitted the theory’s precision-weighting mechanism.

The proposed model uses diffusion models’ hierarchical sampling to estimate precision and then uses those estimates to weight guidance. In the account adopted by the paper, lower-precision signals receive greater attention. The method therefore brings an additional predictive-coding mechanism into the forecasting process, rather than relying only on hierarchical prediction and residual correction.

Experiments on rigid-body and fluid-motion data show that the estimated weights reflect the model’s predictability. The authors also evaluate forecasting on U.K. precipitation and ERA surface wind datasets, reporting improvements over both domain-specific operational models and general deep prediction models. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed weighting mechanism in the evaluated forecasting settings.
icml-2024-cogdpm-diffusion-probabilistic.tldr: CogDPM uses diffusion-derived precision estimates to guide forecasting, with reported gains on motion, precipitation, and surface wind tasks.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects becomes more difficult when outcomes are connected through a network and interference must be accounted for. The paper focuses on bias caused by misspecified models in this setting. It argues that restricted parametric models and neural approaches fitting only one nuisance function can both face problems when the data-generating assumptions are inadequate.

The authors adapt targeted learning to neural-network training under networked interference. They first establish a condition for double robustness, then translate that condition into a targeted training loss. This produces an end-to-end estimator whose training objective is tied to the theoretical requirement, connecting the desired robustness property directly to how the estimator is fitted.

The theoretical analysis gives a faster convergence rate than an approach using a single nuisance model. Experiments on semisynthetic data built from two real-world networks support the proposed estimators’ effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both methodological and theoretical: a way to train causal estimators for network interference, together with an explicit condition governing their double robustness.
icml-2024-doubly-robust-causal-effect-es.tldr: A targeted neural-network loss enables doubly robust causal estimation under network interference, with theoretical and semisynthetic empirical support.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use demonstrations supplied in its prompt without updating its parameters. This paper asks whether the effect of those demonstrations can instead be incorporated into the model itself. For transformers with linearized attention, the authors show that adding bias terms can make that contextual information explicit and permanent.

Their algorithm, ICLCA, converts demonstration prompts into additional biases. The mathematical result establishes equivalence between the prompted linearized model and the same model equipped with those terms. Exactness is the important distinction: in this setting, the conversion preserves the effect of the demonstrations rather than merely learning an approximation through expensive parameter updates.

Experiments demonstrate exact incorporation of context tokens in a linear transformer. The authors also suggest an adaptation for ordinary, nonlinearized transformers, where conversion is approximate. GPT-2 experiments show that the added biases still convey useful context in that case. The paper thus separates an exact result for linearized architectures from an empirically useful approximation for a regular transformer.
icml-2024-exact-conversion-of-in-context.tldr: ICLCA exactly converts demonstration prompts into bias terms for linearized transformers and provides an approximate adaptation tested on GPT-2.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods often judge an input feature by changing it and observing how the model’s prediction responds. A difficulty arises when different features cause similar prediction changes: the perturbation result alone may not distinguish their contributions well. This paper introduces FANS to make those distinctions using necessity and sufficiency.

FANS searches for a neighborhood around the input in which perturbations have a high probability of being both necessary and sufficient causes of prediction changes. It uses that probability as the feature-importance score. The neighborhood is estimated heuristically, and the score is computed through a two-stage perturbation procedure involving factual and interventional reasoning.

To construct the counterfactual samples needed by this procedure, the method resamples observed examples to approximate the relevant conditional distribution. The authors report that FANS outperforms existing attribution methods on six benchmarks. Its contribution is a more discriminating attribution criterion, implemented through neighborhood estimation and counterfactual approximation, for cases where ordinary prediction-change tests give similar scores to different features.
icml-2024-feature-attribution-with-neces.tldr: FANS scores feature importance through estimated necessity and sufficiency, using two-stage perturbations and resampled counterfactuals.

paragraphs: A diagnosis can enter a dataset only after someone decides to order a test. If untested people are then recorded as disease-free, the labels mix health status with testing decisions. This paper studies disparate censorship, where that labeling process differs across subgroups. Training directly on these labels can amplify the bias already present in who receives testing.

The authors propose Disparate Censorship Expectation-Maximization, or DCEM, to learn under this specific form of biased observation. The algorithm is motivated by causal models of selective labels. Its purpose is to account for the decision process behind observed labels rather than treating every recorded negative as equally informative about the underlying outcome.

The paper theoretically analyzes how DCEM mitigates effects on model performance. On synthetic data, it reduces bias measured by the area between ROC curves while maintaining discriminative performance measured by AUC relative to baselines. A clinical sepsis-classification task produces similar results. These findings support addressing unequal label observation without necessarily sacrificing the model’s ability to distinguish outcomes.
icml-2024-from-biased-selective-labels-t.tldr: DCEM addresses subgroup-dependent missing labels, reducing measured bias without sacrificing discrimination in synthetic and clinical sepsis experiments.

paragraphs: A language model can give a correct answer and then abandon it when a user challenges the response. The paper treats this as a form of sycophancy: prioritizing agreement with the user over accuracy. Conventional supervised fine-tuning can reduce this behavior, but the authors identify degradation of general capabilities as a recurring tradeoff.

Supervised pinpoint tuning, or SPT, addresses the problem by first identifying and verifying a small set of modules that strongly affect the targeted behavior. These modules account for less than 5% of the model’s basic modules. Training then updates only that selected set while keeping the rest of the model frozen.

The reported experiments show substantial reductions in sycophancy, including better mitigation than conventional supervised fine-tuning, with limited or no side effects on general capabilities. The result supports selective intervention as a way to improve a particular behavior while retaining broader abilities. It also links behavioral analysis to training: identifying influential modules determines where the corrective updates are applied.
icml-2024-from-yes-men-to-truth-tellers-.tldr: Supervised pinpoint tuning reduces sycophancy by updating a verified subset of modules, with limited or no observed damage to general capabilities.

paragraphs: Interpretable graph neural networks often assign importance to nodes or edges and extract a smaller subgraph to explain a prediction. This paper asks whether those architectures can represent the relationships needed to recover the intended explanatory subgraph. It identifies a gap between producing importance scores and having sufficient representational power for interpretable subgraph learning.

The authors formalize the problem using a subgraph multilinear extension, called SubMT, which represents the subgraph distribution in their framework. Accurate approximation of SubMT is required to extract the desired explanation. They show that existing methods can approximate it poorly, and that this failure can degrade the interpretability of the selected subgraphs.

They introduce Graph Multilinear neT, or GMT, with provably greater power to approximate SubMT. Experiments support the theoretical findings across 12 regular and geometric graph benchmarks, reporting improvements of up to 10% in interpretability and generalizability over the state of the art. The contribution connects explanation quality to a specific representational requirement and designs an architecture around that requirement.
icml-2024-how-interpretable-are-interpre.tldr: GMT improves graph explanations by addressing a theoretically identified approximation gap in existing interpretable graph neural networks.

paragraphs: An instruction-following language model can perform very differently depending on how a task is phrased. Finding a good instruction becomes harder when the model is accessible only as a black box and gradients cannot be used. InstructZero tackles this by searching through an open-source model that generates instructions for the target model.

The search operates on a low-dimensional soft prompt rather than directly editing discrete instruction text. At each step, the open-source model turns that soft prompt into an instruction. The instruction is evaluated on the black-box model in a zero-shot setting, and the resulting performance feeds a Bayesian optimization procedure that proposes subsequent soft prompts.

This arrangement connects a continuous search space to usable natural-language instructions, with target-model evaluations guiding the process. The authors test different combinations of open-source models and APIs, including Vicuna and ChatGPT. They report improvements over state-of-the-art automatic instruction methods across varied downstream tasks, supporting the use of an accessible model as an intermediary for optimizing instructions to an inaccessible one.
icml-2024-instructzero-efficient-instruc.tldr: InstructZero uses Bayesian optimization and an open-source language model to discover better instructions for a black-box model.

paragraphs: Rich datasets can support useful machine learning while also exposing sensitive information about people. Removing sensitive information can damage other useful properties, and heuristic transformations may provide little theoretical guidance about that tradeoff. MaSS formulates the problem in information-theoretic terms and develops a learned transformation designed to suppress selected sensitive attributes.

The framework aims to retain other useful attributes even when those attributes were not specified or explicitly labeled for preservation. This matters because a dataset’s future uses need not be fully known when privacy protection is applied. The objective is selective suppression: reducing designated sensitive information while keeping the transformed data useful more broadly.

The authors analyze the framework’s operational bounds and evaluate it across facial images, voice recordings, and human-activity motion sensor signals. They report effectiveness and generalizability across multiple tasks and configurations. The work combines a formal account of the suppression-and-utility problem with evidence across different data types, supporting a learned approach to preserving utility beyond a predefined list of retained attributes.
icml-2024-mass-multi-attribute-selective.tldr: MaSS learns to suppress selected sensitive attributes while preserving useful information, including attributes not explicitly designated for retention.

paragraphs: Using a multimodal language model as an evaluator requires knowing whether its judgments reflect human preferences. This paper introduces MLLM-as-a-Judge, a benchmark for examining that ability across vision-language tasks. It separates evaluation into assigning scores, comparing pairs, and ranking batches, allowing different forms of judgment to be assessed individually.

The results vary substantially by task. Models show strong human-like discernment when comparing two alternatives, but their scores and batch rankings diverge significantly from human preferences. That distinction matters because success at choosing between two responses does not, by itself, establish that the same model will assign suitable scores or produce human-aligned rankings.

Further analysis finds biases, hallucinated responses, and inconsistent judgments, including in GPT-4V. These are observed problems with evaluative reliability, not merely differences in how results are presented. The authors therefore call for improvements before treating multimodal models as fully reliable evaluators. The benchmark provides a way to examine that reliability through several distinct judgment tasks rather than a single aggregate impression.
icml-2024-mllm-as-a-judge-assessing-mult.tldr: Multimodal models align better with human preferences in pair comparisons than in scoring or batch ranking, while retaining substantial judgment failures.

paragraphs: Online decision problems differ in how much feedback a choice reveals. This paper studies a setting between expert advice and multi-armed bandits: options are divided into groups, and choosing one option reveals the losses of every option in its group. The group sizes determine how informative each observation can be.

For T rounds and group sizes m₁ through mK, the authors prove that minimax regret scales as the square root of T times the sum of log(mk + 1). Matching upper and lower bounds establish the optimal order of this dependence. The result captures how both the number of groups and their sizes affect achievable decision performance.

The paper also gives an optimal pure-exploration algorithm for identifying an approximately best option. At the stated confidence level, its sample requirement scales with that same logarithmic sum divided by the squared accuracy tolerance. Extensions to graph feedback use clique covers and related graph parameters, yielding tight regret bounds for several graph families and connecting grouped observations to more general feedback structures.
icml-2024-on-interpolating-experts-and-m.tldr: The paper derives optimal regret and exploration bounds when choosing an option reveals feedback for an entire group of options.

paragraphs: A graph generator should reproduce meaningful structure while producing diverse outputs rather than repeating its training graphs. This paper examines the tradeoff between structural representation and training-data overlap. It organizes graph generators into a nested hierarchy with edge-independent, node-independent, and arbitrarily dependent levels, covering a wide range of existing methods.

The authors derive bounds on how many triangles and other short cycles each level can produce. Their analysis shows that richer dependency structures allow a better tradeoff between representational power and overlap. They also construct examples establishing asymptotic optimality of the bounds, showing that the theoretical limits can be attained in the corresponding asymptotic sense.

Alongside the theory, the paper introduces generators at all three levels using dense-subgraph discovery. Evaluations on real-world datasets compare both output quality and overlap with popular graph generators. The proposed simple, interpretable models perform competitively. The broader contribution is an evaluation framework that treats structural accuracy and edge diversity as linked properties, making the role of dependency assumptions explicit.
icml-2024-on-the-role-of-edge-dependency.tldr: Richer edge dependencies improve the theoretical tradeoff between reproducing graph structure and avoiding excessive overlap with training data.

paragraphs: Adaptive binary testing identifies an unknown state through a sequence of yes-or-no observations. Each result helps determine the next test, and testing stops when confidence is sufficient or tests run out. Finding the strategy with the smallest expected test count is generally difficult, so Information Maximization, or InfoMax, greedily selects the test with the largest information gain.

This paper gives tight, non-vacuous performance bounds under a specific availability assumption. At every iteration, some remaining test must have a conditional probability of a true outcome within δ of one-half. The requirement ensures that a reasonably balanced test remains available given the outcomes already observed; the guarantees depend on this condition.

The analysis covers both tests determined by the unknown state and tests corrupted by a binary symmetric channel. For modest δ values, the bounds establish near-optimal performance, with average test counts controlled by a small multiple of the state’s entropy. The result supplies a conditional theoretical explanation for the practical efficiency of a widely used greedy strategy.
icml-2024-performance-bounds-for-active-.tldr: InfoMax receives tight near-optimal testing guarantees when a sufficiently balanced binary test remains available at every step.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning methods face different difficulties depending on task structure. Value-function learning struggles when rewards are sparse and success requires a long sequence of decisions, because credit assignment and extrapolation errors become harder to manage. Methods specialized for long-horizon, goal-conditioned tasks can perform worse in shorter tasks with frequent rewards.

PlanDQ combines two approaches in a hierarchical planner. At the high level, a diffusion-based D-Conductor proposes subgoals that guide the policy. At the low level, a Q-learning-based Q-Performer works to accomplish those subgoals. This division gives long-range planning and local execution distinct roles within the same offline learning system.

Experiments suggest superior or competitive performance on D4RL continuous-control benchmarks and on the long-horizon AntMaze, Kitchen, and Calvin tasks. These results support the proposed combination across the evaluated task types, rather than establishing universal superiority. The paper’s contribution is a practical architecture for bridging the performance gap between methods suited to sparse, delayed rewards and those effective with shorter horizons and denser rewards.
icml-2024-plandq-hierarchical-plan-orche.tldr: PlanDQ combines diffusion-based subgoal planning with Q-learning execution to achieve competitive results across short- and long-horizon offline RL tasks.

paragraphs: An environment model learned from one collection of behavior policies can become inaccurate when used to evaluate a different policy. This matters because policy evaluation and optimization depend on predicting what that policy will experience. The paper proposes conditioning the learned dynamics model on a representation of the policy being evaluated.

This policy-conditioned model, or PCM, learns to adapt its predictions to the target policy’s state-action distribution. The authors describe it as a meta-dynamics model that adjusts to the evaluation policy. They find this especially useful when the offline dataset contains diverse behavior policies, providing a setting in which policy-aware model learning can mitigate prediction mismatch.

The paper supplies an algorithm, theoretical analysis, and experimental evidence for reducing policy-value gaps through this adaptation. PCM reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art off-policy evaluation methods by a large margin on DOPE. It also produces better policies in offline policy selection and model predictive control than standard model learning. The findings support adapting the learned model to its downstream policy-evaluation use.
icml-2024-policy-conditioned-environment.tldr: Conditioning environment models on the evaluation policy improves reported prediction, policy evaluation, and policy selection results.

paragraphs: Reordering the premises of a reasoning problem can leave its underlying meaning unchanged. This paper shows that language-model performance can nevertheless change sharply. It investigates sensitivity to presentation order as a weakness that may be hidden when evaluations use only one arrangement of the same information.

In deductive reasoning, the models perform best when premises appear in the order needed by the intermediate proof steps. Presenting them in the ground-truth proof order substantially improves accuracy compared with random ordering. Across the evaluated models, rearranging premises can cause performance drops exceeding 30%, even when results are respectable under the most favorable order.

The authors also introduce R-GSM, a benchmark derived from GSM8K that tests ordering effects in mathematical problem solving. Accuracy again falls significantly relative to the original benchmark. Together, the findings show that the organization of supplied information affects measured reasoning performance in both settings. They also make clear that success with a helpful ordering can coexist with brittleness to an equivalent reordering.
icml-2024-premise-order-matters-in-reaso.tldr: Language-model reasoning accuracy can fall sharply when premises are reordered, despite the underlying problem remaining unchanged.

paragraphs: Forecasting a dynamical system can require a distribution of possible futures rather than one predicted state. This paper formulates forecasting as sampling the future state conditional on the current state. It uses stochastic interpolants to construct a generative process that transforms the present observation into an ensemble of possible forecasts.

The constructed dynamics are fictitious rather than a physical model of the system. In the theoretical construction, they start at the current state and reach the target conditional distribution in finite time without bias. The authors prove that the stochastic differential equation’s drift is nonsingular and can be learned from time-series data using squared-error regression.

Both drift and diffusion can be adjusted after training. A particular adjustment minimizing the impact of estimation error produces a Föllmer process, connecting the sampling design to robustness against learned-model error. Demonstrations include stochastically forced Navier–Stokes systems and video prediction on KTH and CLEVRER. The contribution combines a conditional sampling construction with a learnable forecasting procedure and post-training flexibility.
icml-2024-probabilistic-forecasting-with.tldr: A learned stochastic process turns the current system state into probabilistic forecasts, with post-training adjustments that can reduce estimation-error impact.

paragraphs: Foundation models appear to learn relationships among objects, but prediction-focused statistical descriptions may not fully capture that structured knowledge. This paper proposes a mathematical framework for studying relational learning during pretraining. Its central move is to represent the world as a hypergraph and treat learning as recovery of that underlying structure.

Within the framework, observed data are random samples from hyperedges. The theoretical questions are whether a pretrained model can recover the hypergraph and how efficiently it can do so from data. The authors analyze feasibility and data efficiency using a minimax, near-optimal perspective, making relational recovery an explicit object of study rather than leaving it implicit in prediction accuracy.

The framework brings graph-theoretic tools into the analysis of pretrained models and is presented as applicable to multiple scenarios. As an example, the authors extend it to entity alignment in multimodal learning. The contribution is a theoretical lens for understanding how observations can reveal structured relations, with a concrete extension showing how that lens can organize a multimodal learning problem.
icml-2024-relational-learning-in-pre-tra.tldr: The paper models relational pretraining as hypergraph recovery and analyzes when recovery is feasible and data-efficient.

paragraphs: Diffusion models have been used to remove adversarial disturbances or generate training data, but the paper identifies weaknesses in both routes. Purification can be defeated by stronger adaptive attacks, while adversarial training can struggle with unfamiliar threats. Robust Diffusion Classifier, or RDC, instead builds a generative classifier from a pretrained diffusion model.

RDC first optimizes an input to increase its data likelihood. It then estimates class-conditional likelihoods using the diffusion model and applies Bayes’ theorem to obtain class probabilities. To reduce computational cost, the authors introduce a multi-head diffusion backbone and more efficient sampling strategies. The classifier does not require training against particular adversarial attacks.

The authors demonstrate generalization across multiple unseen threats. On CIFAR-10, they report 75.67% robust accuracy against the evaluated adaptive attacks bounded by an ℓ∞ perturbation of 8/255, a 4.77% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art adversarial training models. These results support the potential of diffusion-based generative classification for robustness in the tested setting, including threats outside attack-specific training.
icml-2024-robust-classification-via-a-si.tldr: RDC uses diffusion-model likelihoods for robust classification and reports strong results against adaptive and previously unseen adversarial threats.

paragraphs: Self-Play Fine-Tuning, or SPIN, aims to improve a language model without collecting additional human annotations. It begins with a model that has already undergone supervised fine-tuning and continues to use the existing human demonstration data. The new training signal comes from responses generated by earlier iterations of the model itself.

The model improves by learning to distinguish those self-generated responses from the human demonstrations. Repeating this process makes previous versions of the model part of the training mechanism. The authors prove that the training objective reaches its global optimum only when the model’s policy matches the target data distribution; this characterizes the optimum rather than guaranteeing every training run reaches it.

Evaluations include the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard, MT-Bench, and Big-Bench datasets. SPIN significantly improves performance across several benchmarks and can outperform models trained with direct preference optimization using additional GPT-4 preference data. These results support making better use of existing demonstrations through iterative self-play, with the paper presenting broader human-level performance as a promise of the approach.
icml-2024-self-play-fine-tuning-converts.tldr: SPIN improves a supervised language model through iterative self-play using existing human demonstrations and responses from earlier model versions.

paragraphs: Bootstrapped value estimation learns from targets that themselves depend on estimated values. With function approximation and off-policy data, establishing convergence can be difficult. This paper proves that combining a target network with over-parameterized linear function approximation yields a weaker convergence condition in certain cases, including settings with off-policy observations.

The condition is naturally satisfied for expected updates over the full state-action space and for batches of complete trajectories from episodic Markov decision processes. Using only a target network or only over-parameterization does not provide the same guarantee. The result therefore concerns their joint effect within the analyzed linear approximation setting.

The authors extend the analysis to truncated trajectories, where minor modifications resembling value truncation at final trajectory states enable convergence for all tasks covered by that extension. Their main prediction result includes high-probability value-error bounds and experiments on Baird’s counterexample and a Four-room task. They also examine control, showing that similar convergence conditions apply to Q-learning. Together, these results identify concrete conditions under which the combination stabilizes learning.
icml-2024-target-networks-and-over-param.tldr: Target networks and over-parameterized linear models jointly provide convergence guarantees for bootstrapped value learning under the paper’s stated conditions.

paragraphs: Real machine learning systems often contain multiple trainable components alongside black-box operations. Optimizing the whole system is difficult because there may be millions of parameters and no analytical expression for overall behavior. This paper calls the joint optimization problem AutoAI and proposes A-BAD-BO to exploit the structure available inside individual components.

The method uses each component’s local loss as an auxiliary indicator of system performance. Bayesian optimization searches over a lower-dimensional configuration of these losses. The differentiable structure of the machine learning components then connects that optimized configuration back to system parameters, combining system-level search with component-level optimization.

The authors establish asymptotic no regret and use it to show convergence to optimal system parameters. They also evaluate synthetic and real-world systems, including a language-model prompt-engineering pipeline with millions of parameters. Reported results show better system optimality than gradient-driven baselines and greater sample efficiency than pure Bayesian optimization. The contribution is a way to coordinate many trainable parameters while reserving black-box search for a smaller space.
icml-2024-towards-autoai-optimizing-a-ma.tldr: A-BAD-BO combines Bayesian optimization over local-loss configurations with differentiable component training to optimize complex machine learning systems.
